part_title: Cloud Foundations — How the Internet and Servers Work
review_basis: Reviewed all original AIF Module 02 WebP slides 01–06 showing client-server requests, postal networking analogy, server hardware, routers and switches, data centers and traditional-IT challenges.

scenes.title: How a website request reaches a server
scenes.narration: Before we learn cloud computing, let's see what happens when you open a website. Begin on the left with a laptop. In this picture, your laptop is the client. A client is the device or program that asks another system for something. The web server on the right is a computer running the software that responds to website requests. In step one, you type a website name in the browser. A name like example dot com is easier for a person to remember than a numerical Internet Protocol address, or IP address. A system called DNS, the Domain Name System, helps the browser discover the address for the website. DNS is like looking up the correct destination in a contact list. The request then travels through the internet, shown in the center as many connected networks, not as one giant computer. Routers and other network devices help data travel toward the destination. In step three the server receives the request and determines which website or application is being requested. In step four the server sends a response. Your browser takes the received information and displays the page. The dashed blue arrow shows the return trip. A website may involve more than one server, but this simple client-and-server path is the foundation. Think of ordering food: you place a request, someone prepares the result, and the answer comes back to you. The difference is that network traffic moves using addressing and communication protocols. Here is a quick check: is the web server inside your browser? No. The browser requests content, and the server responds. Later, cloud services let us run those servers without buying the physical machines ourselves.

scenes.title: Networks and addressing: a postal analogy
scenes.narration: This illustration uses an ordinary postal system to explain computer networking. Look at the first panel, where a house has a mailbox labeled one two three Maple Street. An address identifies where a letter should be delivered. On a computer network, an IP address plays a similar role for network communication. It identifies a device or network destination within the relevant addressing system. The address does not tell us what the message contains. Next, look at the truck traveling along roads between different locations. The roads represent interconnected networks that carry information from a sender toward a destination. Data on networks is usually divided into small units called packets, and network devices help forward them. You don't need to memorize packet formats yet. The third panel shows a letter arriving at the matching mailbox. The key lesson is that the correct destination address and a working path are both necessary. Having an address does not guarantee communication if the network is disconnected, or if access is blocked by a security rule. This is also why people use domain names like a university website: the name is human-friendly, and DNS can help find the relevant IP address. The postal comparison is useful, but not exact. Computers also use protocols and ports so information reaches the appropriate program on the destination device. We will meet those terms later. Imagine a student wants to connect from a laptop to an online course portal. What must be true? The laptop needs a working network connection, and it needs a way to identify and reach the portal's destination. Networking connects locations; addressing helps information reach the right one.

scenes.title: Inside a server: compute, memory, storage and networking
scenes.narration: Now look inside the server itself. The top row shows five building blocks that work together. The first is compute, represented by the CPU. CPU means central processing unit. It carries out instructions from programs, like checking a username or calculating the price of items in an online shopping cart. The second block is memory, or RAM. RAM holds data that the running application needs quickly. Think of RAM as the desk space where you keep the papers you are actively working with. The third block is storage, shown as a solid-state drive. Storage holds files and data over time, including when the server is switched off. A useful analogy is a cupboard where those papers can be stored for later. The fourth block is a database, which is software that organizes and manages records, such as product names, prices and orders. A database uses compute, memory and storage; it is not simply another physical chip like the CPU. The fifth block is networking, which connects the server to other devices and services. Follow the center-left arrows: a customer's browser sends a request across the internet, through a router connecting networks and a switch linking local devices, toward the server. Now follow the six-step product-page example at the bottom. The user requests a product, network devices carry the request, the CPU runs application code, RAM holds temporary working information, the database reads product records, and the server returns the page. These tasks happen together very quickly. For a quick test, which component keeps a product's price saved after power is turned off? Persistent storage and the database built on it, not temporary RAM. Cloud computing offers all of these capabilities as services.

scenes.title: Core IT terms: networks, databases and servers
scenes.narration: This slide revisits the same web request, but this time concentrates on the names of the network devices. In the first panel, a network is any connected group of devices that can communicate and exchange information. It might be your home's Wi-Fi network or an organization's office network. In panel two, a router connects different networks and decides where to forward traffic next. Your home router helps devices communicate beyond the home network through an internet connection. In panel three, a switch connects devices within a local network. Think of the switch as helping messages reach the correct desk within an office, while the router helps those messages travel between offices. In panel four, the server runs an application, and the database stores and organizes the records that application uses. Follow the big arrows from left to right. The laptop is the client. Its local network leads through a switch and router to the internet. On the far right, a company network contains a server and database. The example at the bottom goes through three stages: your device sends a request, the network forwards it toward the appropriate server, and the application retrieves data and sends a response. Real networks can contain many additional components, so this is a teaching model rather than a blueprint of every connection. Here's a practical question: if a company needs to store student marks and retrieve them by student number, should it put the values into a router? No. A router moves network traffic. The student records belong in an application and database. Distinguishing these roles will make AWS services much easier to understand.

scenes.title: From a home server to a data center
scenes.narration: Before the cloud became popular, organizations commonly bought and operated their own computers to run applications. This picture shows how that responsibility grows. On the left is a home or garage server. It might be one computer running a small application for a class project. It is inexpensive to begin, but its capacity is limited, and a power failure can stop the service. The middle panel shows an office server room. Now several servers may run applications for many employees. Someone must maintain the equipment, monitor it, make backups, manage network connections and arrange power and cooling. On the right is a data center. This is a facility built to house many servers, with racks of computers, specialized cooling, high-speed networks, physical security and backup power. UPS means uninterruptible power supply, which helps keep equipment running through some interruptions. The bottom business example shows a company growing from one server to several racks as its customer count increases. More servers allow more work, but they also demand more spending and technical staff. Finally, the bottom-right comparison introduces an important cloud principle. A cloud provider such as AWS operates the physical infrastructure; the customer chooses and configures services and still manages responsibilities such as application code, data, access control and cost. The exact division depends on the service. Cloud does not mean the customer has no security duties. Imagine a small graduate-led startup launching a website. Would it rather buy a data center immediately, or rent the computing resources it needs while it grows? Renting from a cloud provider can reduce the physical operating burden, but the team must still use the resources responsibly.

scenes.title: The challenges of traditional IT
scenes.narration: This slide compares running your own traditional data center with using a cloud provider. Look at the left image: rows of physical servers, cooling equipment, electrical systems and staff. An organization that owns this infrastructure must purchase hardware, keep it maintained and replace equipment when it fails. The center lists five common difficulties. First, high upfront and ongoing cost: the organization pays for equipment, facilities, electricity, cooling and support. Second, slow change: if demand grows suddenly, buying and installing servers can take time. Third, limited scalability: a server can only handle the amount of work its hardware supports. Scalability means the ability to handle more or less workload by adjusting resources. Fourth, constant operational effort: teams must monitor equipment, handle failures and maintain backups. Finally, physical risks such as fire, power loss or severe weather must be managed. The right picture shows a cloud provider running infrastructure for customers. With cloud computing, organizations can request compute, storage or networking resources without individually purchasing every underlying machine. That can make scaling faster and replace some upfront capital spending with service charges, but it does not remove all costs or operational work. Customers still configure security, protect data and avoid unnecessary spending. The example at the bottom describes a growing company waiting weeks or months for traditional capacity. Cloud may be a strong option when quicker access to computing resources matters. However, cloud isn't always the cheapest or best choice for every workload. Later we will compare cost, flexibility, compliance and reliability. A question to remember: if a company wants to run an AI experiment for only a few days, would purchasing permanent servers always make sense? Not necessarily. Cloud services can provide temporary capacity, making it easier to experiment while controlling the resources used.
